questions.enonce_markdown:
Outline any FOUR features of the following retail shops:

(i) Hypermarkets.

(ii) Consumer co-operatives societies.

(8 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** A **retail shop** sells goods in small quantities to final consumers. Hypermarkets and consumer co-operative societies are two types of retail business with different features.

**(i) Hypermarkets (any four features)**

1. **Very large selling area**, usually on the edge of a town, with a big car park.
2. **Wide range of goods under one roof**: food, clothes, electrical goods, furniture, household items.
3. **Self-service and cash payment at checkout points**; the customer picks the goods and pays on leaving.
4. **Low prices** thanks to bulk buying from producers and fast turnover of stock.
5. **Extra services** such as free parking, restaurants, a bank and delivery of heavy goods; open for long hours.

**(ii) Consumer co-operative societies (any four features)**

1. **Owned and run by the members**, who are the consumers; they buy shares to join and each member has **one vote** whatever the number of shares.
2. **Democratic control**: members elect a committee that manages the society.
3. **Profits (surplus) are shared** among the members as a **dividend on purchases** (a bonus in proportion to what each member spent) and part is kept for the society.
4. **Open membership**: any person may join and members are encouraged to buy from the society.
5. **Limited liability**: members lose only the value of the shares they hold; the society has a legal existence of its own.

**Conclusion.** The hypermarket is owned by investors and aims at profit through volume sales; the consumer co-operative is owned by its customers and shares its surplus among them.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Study the information provided in the table and answer the questions that follows:

| SHOP | TURNOVER (CFAF) | AVERAGE STOCK (CFAF) | GROSS PROFITS (CFAF) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| A | 2,400,000 | 600,000 | 1,200,000 |
| B | 2,700,000 | 900,000 | 1,000,000 |

Calculate for each shop:

(i) Rate of turnover.

(ii) Margin.

(6 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** Two ratios are used to compare the shops. The **rate of stock turnover** shows how many times the average stock is sold and replaced during the period; it is found from the cost of goods sold. The **margin** is the gross profit expressed as a percentage of the turnover (sales).

First find the **cost of goods sold** (turnover less gross profit):

- Shop A: $2\,400\,000 - 1\,200\,000 = 1\,200\,000$ CFAF
- Shop B: $2\,700\,000 - 1\,000\,000 = 1\,700\,000$ CFAF

**(i) Rate of turnover**

$$
\text{Rate of turnover} = \frac{\text{cost of goods sold}}{\text{average stock}}
$$

- Shop A: $\dfrac{1\,200\,000}{600\,000} = 2$ times
- Shop B: $\dfrac{1\,700\,000}{900\,000} = 1.89$ times (to 2 decimal places)

**(ii) Margin**

$$
\text{Margin} = \frac{\text{gross profit}}{\text{turnover}} \times 100
$$

- Shop A: $\dfrac{1\,200\,000}{2\,400\,000} \times 100 = 50\%$
- Shop B: $\dfrac{1\,000\,000}{2\,700\,000} \times 100 = 37.04\%$ (to 2 decimal places)

| | Shop A | Shop B |
|---|---:|---:|
| Cost of goods sold (CFAF) | 1,200,000 | 1,700,000 |
| Rate of turnover (times) | 2 | 1.89 |
| Margin (%) | 50 | 37.04 |

**Comment.** Shop A turns its stock over more quickly (2 times against 1.89 times) and earns a higher margin (50% against 37.04%), so it is the more efficient shop.

(If the rate of turnover is calculated on turnover instead of cost of goods sold, the values are A = 4 times and B = 3 times; the usual commercial formula uses the cost of goods sold, as above.)

**Answers: (i) A = 2 times, B = 1.89 times; (ii) A = 50%, B = 37.04%.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Briefly explain the following business documents:

(i) An invoice.

(ii) An order.

(iii) Advice note.

(6 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** Business documents are written records that are used at each stage of a sale, from the first request to payment. They give proof of what was agreed.

**(i) An invoice.** An invoice is a document made out by the **seller** and sent to the **buyer**. It lists the goods supplied, their quantity, unit price, any trade discount, the total amount due, the date, and the terms of payment. It is the seller's bill and tells the buyer how much he must pay.

**(ii) An order.** An order (order form or purchase order) is a document made out by the **buyer** and sent to the **seller**. It states exactly the goods wanted (description, quantity, price, delivery date and place). When accepted, it is the contract to supply the goods.

**(iii) Advice note.** An advice note is a document sent by the **seller** to the **buyer**, usually before the goods reach him, to inform him that the goods have been dispatched. It gives the date of dispatch, the carrier and a description of the goods, so the buyer can prepare to receive them.
